Genesis.line: Genesis tells of creation, humanity's fall into sin, and God's covenant promises to Abraham and his family through Joseph's time in Egypt.
more: God creates the world good, but Adam and Eve disobey and sin spreads through their descendants.
God judges the earth with a flood, saves Noah's family, and later scatters the nations at Babel.
God calls Abraham and promises him land, many descendants, and blessing for all nations.
The promise passes to Isaac and then to Jacob, whom God renames Israel.
Joseph is sold into Egypt, rises to power, and saves his family during a famine.

1.line: God creates the heavens, the earth, and all living things in six days, ending with humanity made in his image.
more: God speaks light, sky, land, seas, and plants into being over the first three days.
He fills them with sun, moon, stars, sea creatures, birds, and land animals.
He makes man and woman, blesses them, and gives them rule over the earth.
God sees everything he has made as very good.

2.line: God rests on the seventh day, then forms Adam, places him in Eden, and creates Eve as his partner.
more: God forms the man from dust and breathes life into him.
He forbids eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
Adam names the animals, but none is a fitting helper for him.
God makes the woman from Adam's rib, and the two become one flesh.

3.line: The serpent deceives Eve, she and Adam eat the forbidden fruit, and God judges them and sends them from Eden.
more: Ashamed, they hide from God and blame others when questioned.
God curses the serpent and promises the woman's offspring will crush its head.
Childbirth becomes painful and work becomes toil, ending in death.
God clothes them with skins and guards the way to the tree of life.

4.line: Cain murders his brother Abel and is sent away as a wanderer, and Adam and Eve receive another son, Seth.
more: God accepts Abel's offering but not Cain's, and Cain grows angry.
God puts a mark on Cain to protect him from being killed.
Cain's descendants build a city and develop music and metalworking, while Lamech boasts of violence.
After Seth's son Enosh is born, people begin calling on the Lord's name.

5.line: A genealogy traces Adam's line through Seth to Noah, noting each man's long life and death.
more: Each entry ends with the man's death, showing the curse at work.
Enoch walks with God and is taken without dying.
Methuselah lives longest, and Noah's father Lamech hopes his son will bring relief.

6.line: Humanity grows so wicked that God resolves to send a flood, but he instructs righteous Noah to build an ark.
more: The sons of God take human wives, and the Nephilim appear on the earth.
God regrets making man because the earth is filled with violence.
He gives Noah the ark's dimensions and promises a covenant with him.
Noah is to bring his family and pairs of every animal aboard.

7.line: Noah, his family, and the animals enter the ark, and the flood covers the earth, destroying all other life.
more: Noah takes seven pairs of clean animals and one pair of unclean animals.
Rain falls forty days and nights as the springs of the deep burst open.
The waters prevail on the earth for 150 days.

8.line: God remembers Noah, the waters recede, and Noah leaves the ark and offers sacrifices.
more: The ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat.
Noah sends out a raven and a dove until the dove does not return.
God promises never again to curse the ground or destroy every living creature this way.

9.line: God blesses Noah, makes a covenant never to flood the earth again, and sets the rainbow as its sign.
more: God permits eating meat but forbids blood and requires accountability for murder.
Noah becomes drunk, and Ham sees his nakedness while Shem and Japheth cover him.
Noah curses Ham's son Canaan and blesses Shem and Japheth.
Noah dies at 950 years old.

10.line: The Table of Nations lists the descendants of Noah's sons Japheth, Ham, and Shem and where they settled.
more: Japheth's descendants spread to the coastlands.
Ham's line includes Egypt, Canaan, and Nimrod, a mighty hunter who builds cities in Babylonia and Assyria.
Shem's line leads to Eber, ancestor of the Hebrews.
The list shows how the nations spread across the earth after the flood.

11.line: People build the tower of Babel, God confuses their language and scatters them, and Shem's line leads to Abram.
more: The builders seek to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered.
A genealogy traces Shem's descendants to Terah, father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
Abram's wife Sarai is barren.
Terah takes his family from Ur toward Canaan but settles in Haran and dies there.

12.line: God calls Abram to go to Canaan, promising land, descendants, and blessing, and Abram later goes to Egypt during a famine.
more: Abram travels with Sarai and his nephew Lot, building altars in Canaan.
At Shechem God promises the land to Abram's offspring.
In Egypt, Abram says Sarai is his sister, and Pharaoh takes her.
God strikes Pharaoh's house with plagues, and Pharaoh sends Abram away.

13.line: Abram and Lot separate because their herds are too large, and God renews his promise of land to Abram.
more: Lot chooses the well-watered Jordan Valley and settles near wicked Sodom.
God tells Abram his offspring will be as many as the dust of the earth.
Abram settles at Hebron and builds an altar.

14.line: Abram rescues Lot from invading kings and is blessed by Melchizedek, king of Salem.
more: Four kings defeat the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah and capture Lot.
Abram pursues them with 318 trained men and recovers everyone and everything.
Abram gives Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, a tenth of everything.
He refuses any reward from the king of Sodom.

15.line: God promises Abram a son and countless offspring, Abram believes, and God confirms his covenant in a ceremony.
more: God counts Abram's faith as righteousness.
Abram cuts animals in half, and a smoking pot and flaming torch pass between them.
God foretells four hundred years of slavery for Abram's offspring and their return.
God promises the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.

16.line: Sarai gives her servant Hagar to Abram, Hagar bears Ishmael, and God cares for Hagar in the wilderness.
more: After conceiving, Hagar despises Sarai, who treats her harshly, so Hagar flees.
The angel of the Lord meets her and tells her to return.
He promises Ishmael many descendants and a life of conflict.
Hagar names God the one who sees her.

17.line: God makes circumcision the sign of his covenant, renames Abram and Sarai, and promises that Sarah will bear Isaac.
more: Abram becomes Abraham, meaning father of a multitude, and Sarai becomes Sarah.
Every male in Abraham's household is to be circumcised.
Abraham laughs at the promise of a son in old age.
God promises to bless Ishmael but establishes his covenant with Isaac.

18.line: Three visitors promise Abraham a son within a year, and Abraham pleads with the Lord to spare Sodom.
more: Abraham welcomes the visitors with a generous meal at Mamre.
Sarah laughs in disbelief, and the Lord asks if anything is too hard for him.
God agrees not to destroy Sodom if even ten righteous people are found there.

19.line: Angels rescue Lot's family before God destroys Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot's daughters later conceive by him.
more: The men of Sodom try to assault Lot's guests, and the angels strike them blind.
Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt.
Lot's daughters get him drunk and bear Moab and Ben-ammi, ancestors of Moab and Ammon.

20.line: Abraham again calls Sarah his sister, King Abimelech of Gerar takes her, and God protects her.
more: God warns Abimelech in a dream, and he does not touch Sarah.
Abimelech rebukes Abraham, returns Sarah, and gives him gifts.
Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech's household.

21.line: Sarah gives birth to Isaac, Hagar and Ishmael are sent away, and Abraham makes a treaty at Beersheba.
more: Isaac is circumcised on the eighth day, and Sarah rejoices.
God provides water for Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness and promises Ishmael a great nation.
Abraham and Abimelech swear an oath over a well at Beersheba.

22.line: God tests Abraham by commanding him to sacrifice Isaac, then stops him and provides a ram instead.
more: Abraham takes Isaac to a mountain in Moriah and binds him on the altar.
The angel of the Lord stops him, and Abraham names the place The Lord Will Provide.
God reaffirms his promise because Abraham obeyed.
News comes of the family of Abraham's brother Nahor, including Rebekah.

23.line: Sarah dies, and Abraham buys the field and cave of Machpelah near Hebron from the Hittites to bury her.
more: Abraham insists on paying Ephron the Hittite the full price of four hundred shekels of silver.
The purchase gives Abraham his first legally owned land in Canaan.

24.line: Abraham's servant travels to Mesopotamia, finds Rebekah through God's guidance, and brings her back to marry Isaac.
more: Abraham forbids a Canaanite wife and sends the servant to his relatives.
The servant prays for a sign, and Rebekah offers water to him and his camels.
Her brother Laban agrees, and Rebekah chooses to go.
Isaac marries Rebekah and is comforted after his mother's death.

25.line: Abraham dies, Ishmael's descendants are listed, and Rebekah bears twins Esau and Jacob, who struggle from birth.
more: Abraham's sons by Keturah are sent east, and Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham.
God tells Rebekah the older twin will serve the younger.
Esau, a hunter, sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew.

26.line: God renews his covenant with Isaac, who prospers in Gerar despite conflict over wells.
more: Isaac calls Rebekah his sister, and Abimelech rebukes him when the truth comes out.
The Philistines envy Isaac and stop up his wells, so he moves on.
Abimelech makes a peace treaty with Isaac at Beersheba.
Esau marries two Hittite women, grieving his parents.

27.line: Jacob, helped by Rebekah, deceives his blind father Isaac and receives the blessing intended for Esau.
more: Jacob wears Esau's clothes and goatskins to feel like his hairy brother.
Isaac gives Jacob blessings of abundance and rule over his brothers.
Esau weeps and plans to kill Jacob after Isaac dies.
Rebekah arranges for Jacob to flee to her brother Laban.

28.line: Isaac sends Jacob to Paddan-aram to find a wife, and God appears to Jacob in a dream at Bethel.
more: Esau marries a daughter of Ishmael, hoping to please his father.
Jacob sees a stairway reaching heaven with angels going up and down.
God passes Abraham's promises to Jacob and promises to be with him.
Jacob sets up a stone pillar and vows to give God a tenth.

29.line: Jacob arrives at Laban's home and works seven years for Rachel, but Laban tricks him into marrying Leah first.
more: Jacob meets Rachel at a well and is welcomed by Laban.
Jacob marries Rachel a week later in exchange for seven more years of work.
The Lord sees that Leah is unloved and gives her Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah.

30.line: Rivalry between Rachel and Leah produces more sons, Rachel bears Joseph, and Jacob grows rich despite Laban's scheming.
more: Rachel's servant Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali, and Leah's servant Zilpah bears Gad and Asher.
Leah bears Issachar, Zebulun, and a daughter, Dinah.
Jacob's breeding methods leave him with the strongest flocks.

31.line: Jacob secretly leaves Laban for Canaan, Laban pursues him, and the two make a covenant in Gilead.
more: God tells Jacob to return home, and Rachel steals her father's household gods.
God warns Laban in a dream not to harm Jacob.
Laban searches but does not find the gods Rachel has hidden.
They set up a heap of stones as a witness and part peacefully.

32.line: Jacob fearfully prepares to meet Esau, sends gifts ahead, and wrestles with God, who renames him Israel.
more: Hearing that Esau is coming with four hundred men, Jacob divides his camp and prays.
Jacob wrestles a man all night and will not let go without a blessing.
His hip is put out of joint, and he names the place Peniel.

33.line: Esau warmly welcomes Jacob, the brothers reconcile, and Jacob settles near Shechem.
more: Jacob bows seven times, but Esau runs to embrace him.
Esau accepts Jacob's gifts after Jacob insists.
Jacob buys land at Shechem and builds an altar.

34.line: Shechem violates Dinah, and her brothers Simeon and Levi take revenge by killing the men of his city.
more: Shechem wants to marry Dinah, and his father Hamor proposes intermarriage.
Jacob's sons deceitfully demand that all the city's men be circumcised.
Jacob rebukes Simeon and Levi for endangering the family.

35.line: Jacob returns to Bethel, God reaffirms his name Israel and his promises, and Rachel and Isaac die.
more: Jacob's household gets rid of foreign gods before going to Bethel.
Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin near Bethlehem.
Reuben sleeps with his father's concubine Bilhah.
Jacob's twelve sons are listed, and Esau and Jacob bury Isaac.

36.line: This genealogy lists the descendants of Esau, the Edomites, along with their chiefs and kings.
more: Esau moves with his family to the hill country of Seir, away from Jacob.
The list includes the earlier Horite inhabitants of Seir.
It shows God's promise of nations from Isaac fulfilled through Esau as well.

37.line: Jacob favors Joseph, who dreams of ruling his brothers, and the jealous brothers sell him to traders bound for Egypt.
more: Jacob gives Joseph a richly ornamented robe.
The brothers throw him into a pit, then sell him at Judah's suggestion.
They dip his robe in goat's blood, and Jacob mourns him as dead.
In Egypt, Joseph is sold to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh.

38.line: Judah's widowed daughter-in-law Tamar, denied a husband, disguises herself and conceives twins by Judah, who admits his wrong.
more: Judah's sons Er and Onan die for their wickedness.
Judah withholds his youngest son Shelah from Tamar.
Tamar proves Judah is the father with his seal, cord, and staff.
She bears twin sons, Perez and Zerah.

39.line: Joseph prospers in Potiphar's house but is thrown into prison after rejecting the advances of Potiphar's wife.
more: The Lord is with Joseph, and Potiphar puts him over everything.
Potiphar's wife falsely accuses Joseph using the garment he left behind.
In prison, the Lord gives Joseph favor, and the jailer puts him in charge.

40.line: In prison Joseph interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker, and both come true.
more: The cupbearer is restored to his position within three days.
The baker is hanged, as Joseph predicted.
The cupbearer forgets Joseph.

41.line: Joseph interprets Pharaoh's dreams of coming famine, and Pharaoh makes him ruler over Egypt to prepare for it.
more: Two years later, the cupbearer remembers Joseph when Pharaoh's dreams trouble him.
The dreams foretell seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine.
Joseph stores grain, marries Asenath, and has sons Manasseh and Ephraim.
When famine comes, all the earth buys grain from Joseph.

42.line: Joseph's brothers come to Egypt to buy grain, and Joseph, unrecognized, accuses them of spying and holds Simeon.
more: Ten brothers come, but Jacob keeps Benjamin at home.
Joseph demands they bring Benjamin to prove their honesty.
The brothers see their trouble as punishment for selling Joseph.
Their money is secretly returned in their sacks, alarming them and Jacob.

43.line: The famine forces the brothers to return to Egypt with Benjamin, and Joseph hosts them at a feast.
more: Judah pledges his own life for Benjamin's safety.
Joseph weeps privately when he sees Benjamin.
Benjamin receives a portion five times larger than the others.

44.line: Joseph frames Benjamin with a silver cup, and Judah offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place.
more: Joseph's steward finds the cup in Benjamin's sack.
Judah explains that losing Benjamin would kill their father.
His plea shows the brothers have changed.

45.line: Joseph reveals himself to his brothers, forgives them, and sends for Jacob to come to Egypt.
more: Joseph says God sent him ahead to preserve life.
Pharaoh offers the family the best of the land.
Jacob is stunned to hear Joseph is alive and resolves to see him.

46.line: God reassures Jacob in a vision, and his whole family of seventy moves to Egypt and settles in Goshen.
more: At Beersheba, God promises to make Jacob a great nation in Egypt.
The chapter lists Jacob's descendants who go to Egypt.
Joseph and Jacob have a tearful reunion.

47.line: Jacob meets Pharaoh, and Joseph manages the famine so that the Egyptians sell their land and themselves to Pharaoh.
more: Pharaoh grants the family land in Goshen, and Jacob blesses Pharaoh.
Egyptians trade money, livestock, and land for grain.
Joseph sets a tax of one-fifth of the harvest for Pharaoh.
Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan.

48.line: Jacob adopts and blesses Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, placing the younger ahead of the older.
more: Jacob recalls God's promise to him at Luz.
He crosses his hands to put his right hand on Ephraim.
Jacob gives Joseph an extra portion of land.

49.line: Jacob speaks prophetic words over each of his twelve sons, then dies.
more: Reuben, Simeon, and Levi are rebuked for past sins.
Judah is promised kingship, with the scepter never departing from him.
Joseph receives a rich blessing.
Jacob asks to be buried at Machpelah with his ancestors.

50.line: Joseph buries Jacob in Canaan, reassures his brothers of forgiveness, and dies in Egypt.
more: Egyptians mourn Jacob, and a great procession goes to Canaan for his burial.
Joseph tells his brothers that God meant their evil for good.
Joseph makes Israel swear to carry his bones to the promised land.

Exodus.line: Exodus tells how God rescues Israel from slavery in Egypt, makes a covenant at Sinai, and comes to dwell among them.
more: Israel multiplies in Egypt and is enslaved, and God calls Moses to deliver them.
God sends ten plagues on Egypt, and Israel leaves after the first Passover.
God parts the sea and provides for Israel on the way to Mount Sinai.
At Sinai God gives the Ten Commandments and the laws of the covenant.
Israel worships a golden calf, but God forgives and renews the covenant.
The people build the tabernacle, and God's glory fills it.

1.line: Israel multiplies in Egypt, and a new Pharaoh enslaves them and orders all Hebrew baby boys killed.
more: The new king fears the Israelites will grow too numerous and powerful.
Harsh labor fails to stop their growth.
The Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah fear God and refuse to kill the boys.
Pharaoh then orders every newborn Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile.

2.line: Moses is saved as a baby and raised by Pharaoh's daughter, then flees to Midian after killing an Egyptian.
more: His mother hides him in a basket among the reeds of the Nile.
Grown, Moses kills an Egyptian who is beating a Hebrew.
In Midian he marries Zipporah, daughter of the priest Reuel.
God hears Israel's groaning and remembers his covenant.

3.line: God speaks to Moses from a burning bush and sends him to bring Israel out of Egypt.
more: God reveals himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
He gives his name as I AM WHO I AM.
God promises to bring Israel to a land flowing with milk and honey.
He warns that Pharaoh will resist until God strikes Egypt.

4.line: God gives Moses signs and appoints Aaron as his spokesman, and the Israelites believe Moses' message.
more: Moses' staff becomes a snake, and his hand becomes leprous and is restored.
When Moses objects that he cannot speak well, God angrily appoints Aaron.
On the way, Zipporah circumcises their son when the Lord threatens Moses.
The elders worship when they hear God has seen their affliction.

5.line: Pharaoh refuses to let Israel go and makes their labor harder, and the Israelites blame Moses.
more: Pharaoh says he does not know the Lord.
He orders the slaves to gather their own straw while making the same number of bricks.
Moses complains to God that nothing has improved.

6.line: God reaffirms his covenant and promises to redeem Israel, and the genealogy of Moses and Aaron is given.
more: God declares that he is the Lord and promises to take Israel as his people.
The discouraged Israelites do not listen to Moses.
The genealogy traces Moses and Aaron through the tribe of Levi.

7.line: Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh, Aaron's staff becomes a serpent, and the first plague turns the Nile to blood.
more: God says he will harden Pharaoh's heart and multiply his signs.
Aaron's staff swallows the staffs of Egypt's magicians.
The magicians copy the blood plague, and Pharaoh refuses to listen.

8.line: God sends plagues of frogs, gnats, and flies, and Pharaoh repeatedly promises to release Israel but breaks his word.
more: The magicians cannot copy the gnats and call it the finger of God.
The flies strike Egypt but not Goshen, where Israel lives.
Pharaoh hardens his heart each time relief comes.

9.line: God strikes Egypt with plagues on livestock, boils, and hail, but Pharaoh's heart remains hard.
more: Egypt's livestock die while Israel's are spared.
Boils afflict even the magicians.
Egyptians who fear the Lord's word shelter their servants and animals from the hail.

10.line: Locusts and darkness strike Egypt, and Pharaoh still refuses to let Israel go with all their flocks.
more: Pharaoh's servants urge him to release the people.
Locusts devour everything the hail left.
Thick darkness covers Egypt for three days, but Israel has light.
Pharaoh threatens Moses with death if he returns.

11.line: God announces the final plague, the death of every firstborn in Egypt.
more: The Israelites are to ask the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry.
Moses warns of a great cry throughout Egypt.
Israel will be spared to show that the Lord distinguishes them from Egypt.

12.line: Israel keeps the first Passover, God strikes Egypt's firstborn, and Pharaoh sends Israel out of Egypt.
more: Each household kills a lamb and puts its blood on the doorposts.
The Lord passes over houses marked by the blood.
Israel leaves in haste after 430 years in Egypt, taking Egyptian plunder.
Rules are given for keeping Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread.

13.line: God commands the consecration of the firstborn and leads Israel by a pillar of cloud and fire.
more: Israel is to remember the exodus through Unleavened Bread and redeeming the firstborn.
God leads them toward the Red Sea rather than through Philistine land.
Moses carries Joseph's bones with him.

14.line: Pharaoh pursues Israel, God parts the Red Sea for Israel to cross, and the waters drown Egypt's army.
more: The people panic, but Moses tells them the Lord will fight for them.
Moses stretches out his hand, and a strong east wind divides the waters.
Israel fears the Lord and believes in him and in Moses.

15.line: Moses and Israel sing praise for God's victory at the sea, then God makes bitter water sweet at Marah.
more: The song celebrates the Lord as a warrior who reigns forever.
Miriam leads the women in song and dance.
God promises health if Israel obeys, and they camp at Elim.

16.line: When Israel grumbles about food, God provides quail and daily manna, with a double portion before the Sabbath.
more: Manna must be gathered each morning and spoils if kept overnight.
Some disobey by keeping it or by gathering on the Sabbath.
A jar of manna is kept as a reminder, and Israel eats it forty years.

17.line: God brings water from a rock at Horeb, and Israel defeats the Amalekites while Moses holds up his hands.
more: The place is named Massah and Meribah because the people tested God.
Aaron and Hur support Moses' arms while Joshua fights.
God vows to blot out the memory of Amalek.

18.line: Moses' father-in-law Jethro visits, praises God, and advises Moses to appoint judges to share his burden.
more: Jethro brings Zipporah and Moses' two sons.
He offers sacrifices after hearing what God has done.
Capable, trustworthy men are appointed over groups to judge minor cases.

19.line: Israel arrives at Mount Sinai, God offers them a covenant, and he descends on the mountain in fire and thunder.
more: God calls Israel to be his treasured possession and a kingdom of priests.
The people consecrate themselves for three days.
Boundaries keep the people from touching the mountain.

20.line: God speaks the Ten Commandments, the frightened people ask Moses to mediate, and God gives instructions about altars.
more: The commandments forbid other gods, idols, misuse of God's name, murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting.
They also command Sabbath rest and honoring parents.
Altars are to be made of earth or uncut stone.

21.line: God gives laws on Hebrew servants, violent crimes, and injuries caused by people or animals.
more: Hebrew servants go free in the seventh year unless they choose to stay.
Murder, striking or cursing parents, and kidnapping are punishable by death.
Penalties match the harm done, and owners are liable for dangerous oxen.

22.line: Laws address theft, property damage, and social justice, including protection for widows, orphans, sojourners, and the poor.
more: Thieves must make restitution, and borrowed property must be repaid if lost.
Sorcery, bestiality, and sacrifice to other gods are punishable by death.
Israel must not charge the poor interest and must give God the firstborn.

23.line: Laws require honest justice and Sabbath rest, establish three annual feasts, and promise that God's angel will lead Israel.
more: Israel must not spread false reports or deny justice to the poor.
The land is to rest every seventh year.
The feasts are Unleavened Bread, Harvest, and Ingathering.
God will drive out Canaan's nations little by little.

24.line: Israel accepts the covenant, it is confirmed with blood, and Moses goes up the mountain for forty days.
more: Moses reads the Book of the Covenant, and the people vow obedience.
Moses, Aaron, and seventy elders see God and eat before him.
God's glory covers Sinai like a consuming fire.

25.line: God asks for offerings and gives instructions for the ark of the covenant, the table, and the lampstand.
more: The tabernacle is to be where God dwells among his people.
The ark has a mercy seat with two cherubim, where God will meet Moses.
Everything must follow the pattern shown on the mountain.

26.line: God gives instructions for the tabernacle's curtains, coverings, frames, and the veil that separates the Most Holy Place.
more: Ten linen curtains embroidered with cherubim form the inner covering.
Goat hair and animal skins cover the structure.
The veil screens off the ark from the Holy Place.

27.line: God gives instructions for the bronze altar, the courtyard, and oil for the lamp to burn continually.
more: The altar of burnt offering is acacia wood overlaid with bronze.
Linen hangings on posts enclose the courtyard.
Aaron and his sons must tend the lamp from evening to morning.

28.line: God gives instructions for the priestly garments of Aaron and his sons.
more: The ephod carries two onyx stones engraved with the names of Israel's tribes.
The breastpiece holds twelve stones and the Urim and Thummim.
A gold plate on the turban reads Holy to the Lord.

29.line: God gives instructions for ordaining Aaron and his sons as priests and for the daily burnt offerings.
more: The ordination includes washing, anointing, and sacrifices over seven days.
Blood is placed on the priests' right ear, thumb, and big toe.
God promises to dwell among Israel and be their God.

30.line: God gives instructions for the incense altar, atonement money, the bronze basin, anointing oil, and incense.
more: Each man counted in a census pays half a shekel as a ransom.
Priests must wash at the basin before serving.
The holy oil and incense must not be copied for ordinary use.

31.line: God appoints Bezalel and Oholiab to build the tabernacle and makes the Sabbath a sign of his covenant.
more: God fills Bezalel with his Spirit and skill for craftsmanship.
Profaning the Sabbath is punishable by death.
God gives Moses two stone tablets written by his finger.

32.line: Israel worships a golden calf, and Moses breaks the tablets, punishes the idolaters, and intercedes for the people.
more: Aaron makes the calf when the people grow impatient for Moses.
God threatens to destroy Israel, but Moses pleads and God relents.
The Levites kill about three thousand, and God sends a plague.
Moses offers to be blotted out for the people's sake.

33.line: God says he will not go with Israel, but Moses intercedes, and God promises his presence and reveals his glory.
more: The people mourn and remove their ornaments.
Moses meets God face to face in the tent of meeting outside the camp.
God hides Moses in a cleft of the rock and lets his goodness pass by.

34.line: God renews the covenant on new tablets and proclaims his name, and Moses' face shines from speaking with God.
more: God declares himself merciful and gracious, yet one who punishes guilt.
Israel must not make covenants with Canaanites or worship their gods.
Moses veils his face after speaking to the people.

35.line: Moses calls for Sabbath rest and offerings, and the people generously bring materials for the tabernacle.
more: Men and women bring gold, fabrics, wood, and precious stones.
Skilled women spin yarn and goat hair.
Bezalel and Oholiab are named as the master craftsmen.

36.line: The people give more than enough, and the craftsmen make the tabernacle's curtains, frames, and veil.
more: Moses tells the people to stop bringing offerings.
The work follows God's earlier instructions exactly.

37.line: Bezalel makes the ark, the table, the lampstand, the incense altar, the anointing oil, and the incense.
more: Each item is made of acacia wood and gold as commanded.
The detailed repetition shows careful obedience to God's pattern.

38.line: The bronze altar, the basin, and the courtyard are made, and the materials used are counted.
more: The basin is made from the bronze mirrors of the serving women.
The account lists the gold, silver, and bronze given.
The silver comes from the census of over six hundred thousand men.

39.line: The priestly garments are made, and Moses inspects the finished work and blesses the people.
more: Each garment is made just as the Lord commanded Moses.
The people bring every completed piece to Moses.

40.line: Moses sets up the tabernacle, and the glory of the Lord fills it.
more: It is erected on the first day of the second year after leaving Egypt.
Moses places each item and anoints the tabernacle and the priests.
The cloud by day and fire by night guide Israel's journeys.

Leviticus.line: Leviticus gives God's laws for sacrifice, priesthood, purity, and holy living so that the holy God can dwell among Israel.
more: Five main offerings are described for worship and atonement.
Aaron and his sons are ordained, and two sons die for offering unauthorized fire.
Laws on clean and unclean distinguish what may approach God.
The Day of Atonement cleanses the people and the sanctuary each year.
Further laws call Israel to be holy because God is holy.
Feasts, Sabbath years, the Jubilee, and covenant blessings and curses conclude the book.

1.line: God instructs Moses on burnt offerings from the herd, flock, or birds, wholly burned on the altar.
more: The offerer lays his hand on the animal for acceptance and atonement.
Priests sprinkle the blood and burn the whole sacrifice.
It is a pleasing aroma to the Lord.

2.line: God gives instructions for grain offerings of flour, oil, and frankincense, offered raw or baked.
more: A memorial portion is burned, and the rest goes to the priests.
Grain offerings must contain no leaven or honey.
Every offering is to be seasoned with salt.

3.line: God gives instructions for peace offerings from the herd or the flock.
more: The fat and kidneys are burned on the altar for the Lord.
Israel must not eat fat or blood.

4.line: God gives instructions for sin offerings to atone for unintentional sins by priests, the congregation, leaders, or individuals.
more: The animal required depends on the sinner's position.
For a priest or the congregation, blood is sprinkled before the veil.
The priest makes atonement, and the sinner is forgiven.

5.line: Sin offerings are required for specific failures, with cheaper options for the poor, and guilt offerings for misusing holy things.
more: The sins include withholding testimony, touching uncleanness, and rash oaths.
The poor may bring birds or fine flour.
A guilt offering requires a ram plus restitution with an added fifth.

6.line: Guilt offerings cover wrongs against neighbors, and priests receive instructions for handling the offerings.
more: Deceit or theft requires full restitution plus a fifth and a ram.
The altar fire must never go out.
Priests eat certain portions in a holy place.

7.line: Further instructions cover the guilt offering, the priests' portions, and the rules for peace offerings.
more: Peace offerings may be for thanksgiving, a vow, or a freewill gift.
Anyone unclean who eats a peace offering is cut off from the people.
The breast and right thigh belong to the priests.

8.line: Moses ordains Aaron and his sons as priests in a seven-day ceremony, as God commanded.
more: Moses washes, clothes, and anoints them before the assembly.
He offers a sin offering, a burnt offering, and a ram of ordination.
The priests stay at the entrance of the tent for seven days.

9.line: Aaron offers the first sacrifices as high priest, and fire from the Lord consumes them.
more: He offers sacrifices for himself and for the people.
Aaron blesses the people, and the Lord's glory appears.
The people shout and fall facedown.

10.line: Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire and die, and God gives the priests further rules.
more: Aaron and his remaining sons are told not to mourn publicly.
Priests must not drink wine or strong drink when serving.
They must distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean.

11.line: God distinguishes clean animals Israel may eat from unclean ones they must not eat.
more: Clean land animals chew the cud and have split hooves.
Clean water creatures have fins and scales.
Touching carcasses makes a person unclean, for Israel must be holy.

12.line: A woman is ceremonially unclean after childbirth and offers sacrifices for her purification.
more: Her purification lasts forty days for a son and eighty for a daughter.
A son is circumcised on the eighth day.
She brings a lamb and a bird, or two birds if she is poor.

13.line: Priests examine skin diseases and mildew in fabric to decide whether they are unclean.
more: Suspected cases are isolated and rechecked after seven days.
A person declared unclean lives outside the camp.
Contaminated garments are burned.

14.line: Rituals are given for cleansing those healed of skin disease and houses with spreading mildew.
more: Two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop are used in the cleansing.
Sacrifices follow on the eighth day.
Contaminated stones are removed, and a persistently infected house is torn down.

15.line: Bodily discharges make people unclean, and laws explain how to become clean again.
more: Abnormal discharges require waiting seven days and offering sacrifices.
Normal emissions require washing and waiting until evening.
These laws keep Israel from defiling God's tabernacle.

16.line: God gives instructions for the annual Day of Atonement to cleanse the sanctuary and atone for the people's sins.
more: Aaron enters the Most Holy Place only on this day, with blood and incense.
One goat is sacrificed, and the other carries the people's sins into the wilderness.
The people fast and rest, and the day is a lasting statute.

17.line: Sacrifices must be brought to the tabernacle, and Israel must not eat blood.
more: Sacrificing elsewhere risks offering to goat idols.
The life of the flesh is in the blood, which God gives for atonement.

18.line: God forbids incest, adultery, child sacrifice, homosexual acts, and bestiality, unlike the practices of Egypt and Canaan.
more: Israel must follow God's laws rather than the customs of other nations.
The land vomited out its former inhabitants for these practices.

19.line: God calls Israel to be holy in worship, justice, and love of neighbor, giving varied laws for everyday life.
more: Israel must honor parents, keep Sabbaths, and avoid idols.
Fields must be left partly unharvested for the poor and the sojourner.
They must love their neighbors and sojourners as themselves.
Laws forbid mixing kinds, occult practices, and dishonest measures.

20.line: God sets penalties for Molech worship, consulting mediums, cursing parents, and sexual sins.
more: Many of these offenses carry the death penalty.
God calls Israel to be holy because he has set them apart from the nations.

21.line: God gives priests stricter standards of holiness in mourning, marriage, and physical condition.
more: Priests may mourn only close relatives.
The high priest must marry a virgin from his own people.
Priests with physical defects may eat holy food but not offer sacrifices.

22.line: Priests must handle holy offerings with care, and sacrificial animals must be without defect.
more: Unclean priests may not eat holy food.
Only priests' households may eat the priestly portions.
Animals with defects are not accepted.

23.line: God appoints the Sabbath and Israel's annual feasts as holy convocations.
more: The spring feasts are Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, and Weeks.
Autumn brings Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and Booths.
During Booths, Israel lives in shelters to remember the wilderness.

24.line: Instructions are given for the lamp and the bread of the Presence, and a blasphemer is stoned.
more: Twelve loaves are set before the Lord every Sabbath.
A man of Israelite and Egyptian parentage curses God's name.
God declares that the same laws apply to sojourners and native Israelites.

25.line: God establishes a Sabbath year every seventh year and a Jubilee every fiftieth year.
more: In the Jubilee, land returns to its original families and Israelite servants go free.
The land belongs to God, so it cannot be sold permanently.
Israelites must help poor kinsmen without charging interest.

26.line: God promises blessings for obedience and escalating curses for disobedience, but also restoration if Israel repents.
more: Blessings include rain, peace, and God's presence among them.
Curses include disease, defeat, famine, and exile.
God will remember his covenant if they confess their sin.

27.line: Laws explain how to redeem people, animals, houses, and fields vowed to the Lord, and declare tithes holy.
more: Values for vowed people depend on age and sex.
Things devoted to the Lord cannot be redeemed.
A tenth of produce and flocks belongs to the Lord.
